title: Aviation Vocabulary
text: Aviation Vocabulary Airspeed: The speed of an aircraft relative to its surrounding air mass. Altitude: The height of an aircraft above mean sea level (AMSL). Autopilot: An automatic control system used to guide the aircraft. Beacon: A radio or transponder signal used for directional information or identification. Clearance: Authorization given by Air Traffic Control for an aircraft to proceed under specified conditions. Cockpit: The compartment where the pilot controls the aircraft. Fuselage: The main body of an aircraft. Hangar: A large building where aircraft are stored and maintained. ILS (Instrument Landing System): A system that assists pilots in landing, especially under low visibility. Jet Lag: Fatigue caused by air travel across different time zones. Knot: A unit of speed equal to one nautical mile per hour. Mayday: An international radio distress signal used by aircraft and ships. Nautical Mile: A unit of distance used in aviation and marine navigation. Transponder: An electronic device that transmits a response to an incoming signal. VFR (Visual Flight Rules): Regulations under which a pilot operates an aircraft in weather conditions clear enough to allow visual reference. Wind Shear: A sudden change in wind speed or direction over a short distance. Airfoil: The shape of a wing or blade (of a propeller, rotor, or turbine) designed to produce lift when moving through the air. Taxiway: A path for an aircraft at an airport leading from one part of the airfield to another. Deadhead: A crew member who is on board an aircraft but off-duty. Flaps: Hinged surfaces on the wing of an aircraft, used to reduce speed and increase lift during takeoff and landing. Jetstream: A narrow, variable band of very strong, predominantly westerly air currents encircling the globe several miles above the earth. METAR: A type of weather report used in aviation, giving details about the conditions at an airport. NDB (Non-Directional Beacon): A radio transmitter at a known location, used as an aviation or marine navigational aid. Overhaul: The process of completely inspecting, repairing, and maintaining an aircraft. PAPI (Precision Approach Path Indicator): A visual aid that provides guidance information to help a pilot acquire and maintain the correct approach to an airport or runway. Zulu Time: Another term for Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), the standard time common in aviation. Bulkhead: A dividing wall or barrier in an aircraft's cabin. Crosswind: A wind blowing across the direction of travel, which can affect an aircraft's movement. DME (Distance Measuring Equipment): An electronic device that measures the distance between an aircraft and a ground station. Echo: A code word used in radio communication to represent the letter 'E'. Apron: The area of an airport where aircraft are parked, unloaded or loaded, refueled, or boarded. Canard: A small wing placed forward of the main wing of an aircraft, used to improve stability. Empennage: The tail assembly of an aircraft, including stabilizers, rudder, and elevators. Glide Scope: Part of an Instrument Landing System (ILS), guiding aircraft in descent. Icing: The formation of ice on an aircraft, which can affect performance and safety. Lift: The aerodynamic force that holds an aircraft in the air. Mach: A dimensionless unit representing the speed of an object moving through air, or any fluid substance, divided by the speed of sound. Overwing: The part of an airplane wing that is above the fuselage. Radar: A system that uses radio waves to determine the range, angle, or velocity of objects. Squawk: A four-digit code used by an aircraft's transponder to identify itself to air traffic control radar. Thrust: The force which moves an aircraft through the air. Undercarriage: The landing gear of an aircraft. Vortex: A flow of fluid around a center line, which can affect aircraft, especially during takeoff and landing. Wake Turbulence: Turbulent air left behind an aircraft in flight, which can be hazardous to other aircraft. Yaw: A side-to-side movement of an aircraft's nose. Zero Fuel Weight: The weight of an aircraft with all payloads but without usable fuel. Aileron: A hinged flight control surface usually forming part of the trailing edge of each wing of an aircraft, used to control lateral balance. Bank: The tilting of an aircraft's wings, causing it to turn left or right. Cabin: The enclosed, pressurized part of an airplane where passengers and crew are seated. De-icing: The process of removing ice from the surface of an aircraft, typically before takeoff. levator: A movable control surface in the tail of an aircraft, used to make the nose rise or descend. Final Approach: The last part of an aircraft's approach to landing, following a defined path towards the runway. Groundspeed: The speed of an aircraft relative to the ground. Heading: The direction in which an aircraft's nose is pointed, usually in degrees from North. Instrument Panel: The panel in the cockpit of an aircraft containing flight instruments. Jet: A type of engine that propels aircraft forward by expelling exhaust at high speeds. Kiosk: A small, often temporary, stand or booth at an airport, used for informational or commercial purposes. Landing Gear: The undercarriage of an aircraft, including wheels, used for takeoff and landing. Maintenance: The tasks required to ensure the safe and efficient operation of an aircraft. Navigation: The process or activity of accurately ascertaining one's position and planning and following a route. Oxygen Mask: A device that delivers oxygen to the passengers and crew of an aircraft, especially in emergencies. Pitch: The up or down movement of an aircraft's nose. Queue: A line or sequence of people or vehicles awaiting their turn to be attended to or to proceed. Runway: A long, levelled area, typically paved, at an airport, on which aircraft take off and land. Stall: A sudden loss of lift caused by the flow of air over the wing becoming disrupted. Tailwind: A wind blowing in the same direction as an aircraft's course, increasing its speed. Unicom: A non-control communication facility located at an airport, used for general advisory and communication services. Vertical Speed: The rate at which an aircraft ascends or descends, usually measured in feet per minute. VOR (VHF Omnidirectional Range): A type of short-range radio navigation system for aircraft. Winglet: A small wing-like structure at the tip of an aircraft wing, used to improve efficiency. Acceleration: The rate of change of velocity of an aircraft, including speeding up and slowing down. Black Box: A colloquial term for the flight data recorders and cockpit voice recorders in aircraft. Control Tower: A building at an airport from where air traffic control operates, overseeing aircraft movements. Descent: The act of an aircraft losing altitude, coming down towards landing. Emergency Exit: A specially designed exit used in case of an emergency, particularly in aircraft. ght Deck: The area in the front of the aircraft where the pilot and co-pilot control the aircraft. Glide Path: The descent path of an aircraft as it approaches for landing. Headwind: A wind blowing directly against the direction of an aircraft's motion, slowing its groundspeed. IFR (Instrument Flight Rules): Rules governing the operation of aircraft when the pilot must rely on instruments for navigation due to poor visibility. Jetway: A movable bridge-like structure that connects the airport terminal gate to an aircraft, allowing passengers to board and disembark. Kinetic Energy: The energy an object possesses due to its motion, significant in the context of aircraft movement and impact. Load Factor: A measurement of the stress on an aircraft structure due to the forces of lift, weight, and gravity. Missed Approach: A procedure followed by a pilot when an approach to landing needs to be aborted. No-fly Zone: An airspace in which aircraft are prohibited from flying, typically for security or safety reasons. Overhead Bin: A storage compartment above passenger seats in an aircraft cabin. Propeller: A type of fan that transmits power by converting rotational motion into thrust, commonly used in smaller aircraft. Ramp: The area at an airport where aircraft are parked, loaded, and unloaded, or refueled. Slats: Extendable parts on the leading edge of an aircraft wing, used to increase lift during takeoff and landing. Turbulence: Irregular motion of the air resulting from eddies and vertical currents, causing bumpy flight conditions. Updraft: An upward current of air, often found near terrain like mountains, that can affect an aircraft's altitude. VOR (VHF Omnidirectional Range): A type of radio navigation system for aircraft, helping pilots determine their position and stay on course. Winglet: A small, upward-curving structure at the tip of an aircraft's wing, designed to improve fuel efficiency by reducing drag. Acceleration: The rate at which an aircraft increases its speed. Black Box: Flight recorders used in aircraft to record specific aircraft performance parameters and conversations in the cockpit. Control Tower: A building at an airport from where air traffic controllers manage the safe and orderly flow of aircraft on the ground and in the airspace around the airport. Descent: The phase in flight where the aircraft decreases altitude, approaching the landing phase. Emergency Exit: Special exits used to quickly evacuate an aircraft in an emergency. Flight Deck: The area in the front of the aircraft from which the pilot controls the aircraft. Glide Path: A path in the sky that an aircraft follows during the final descent for landing.
